title: Engineering a Cu/ZnOx Interface for High Methane Selectivity in CO2 Electrochemical Reduction
abstract: An oxidized copper species (Cu) on the metallic copper surface is critical to the activity and selectivity of electrochemical reduction of CO2 gas. However, Cu δ+ species are easily reduced under working conditions of CO2 electroreduction. Herein, we propose an interface engineering strategy to stabilize Cu species; specifically, ZnOx nanoparticles are grown on a copper foil to generate a Cu/ZnOx interface. The interface stabilizes the surface Cu species and delivers high methane selectivity (∼36%) and long-term durability (>12 h) at a potential of −1.1 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) for CO2 reduction. By combining comprehensive characterizations with simulation experiments, we identify cupric species as active sites for CH4 formation, which is confirmed by density functional theory calculations. Our work demonstrates that interface engineering is a promising way to stabilize active sites and boost selective CO2 electroreduction. ■ INTRODUCTION Extreme climate change caused by excessive carbon emission has been regarded as a severe environmental crisis. Converting carbon dioxide into useful energy sources is an effective strategy to alleviate such a global crisis. Among various conversion technologies, an electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CRR) is a simple and manageable technique that can transform CO2 into various energy-dense chemicals such as alkane and olefin. Methane, as an important CRR product, is a fundamental organic chemical raw material for the industrial production of ethylene, acetylene, methanol, etc. Unfortunately, CO2 electroreduction to methane suffers from multistep reactions, high kinetic barriers, and a competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), leading to a low conversion rate, high energy consumption, and poor methane selectivity. Therefore, designing a CRR catalyst with high selectivity toward methane is of great importance to develop such a promising conversion technology. Thus far, a Cu catalyst is still the most active metal for reducing CO2 to hydrocarbons, owing to its unique electronic properties. Nevertheless, pure copper shows poor selectivity to a single hydrocarbon and inescapable hydrogen evolution activity, causing a high cost for separation and collection of the mixed product. To achieve high selectivity to certain desirable reduction products, the chemical state of the copper surface is engineered to tune the adsorption strength of intermediates on the catalyst. Recent studies suggest that the oxidation state of copper on the catalyst surface has a significant influence on the CRR pathway and the product composition. Compared with metallic Cu, the oxidized copper species (Cu) exhibit higher binding strengths to Cbound intermediates, which promotes the activation of CO2 and the subsequent hydrogenation. Our previous study on Cu4.16CeOx catalysts have demonstrated that cuprous ions facilitate the yield rate of ethylene, while cupric ions are related to methane production. Hopefully, methane selectivity can be tuned by controlling the oxidation state of copper. However, surface Cu sites are readily reduced to Cu under CRR working conditions, especially at high reducing potentials, leading to the obvious drop in C1 or C2+ production. Over the past few years, several strategies have been proposed to stabilize the Cu species, including plasma treatment, element doping, support effect, ligand effect, and space limiting effect; nevertheless, the active Cu species are still reduced easily after the prolonged electroreduction. ■ INTRODUCTION Extreme climate change caused by excessive carbon emission has been regarded as a severe environmental crisis. Converting carbon dioxide into useful energy sources is an effective strategy to alleviate such a global crisis.1,2 Among various conversion technologies, an electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CRR) is a simple and manageable technique that can transform CO2 into various energy-dense chemicals such as alkane and olefin.3−6 Methane, as an important CRR product, is a fundamental organic chemical raw material for the industrial production of ethylene, acetylene, methanol, etc.7,8 Unfortunately, CO2 electroreduction to methane suffers from multistep reactions, high kinetic barriers, and a competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER),9 leading to a low conversion rate, high energy consumption, and poor methane selectivity. Therefore, designing a CRR catalyst with high selectivity toward methane is of great importance to develop such a promising conversion technology. Thus far, a Cu catalyst is still the most active metal for reducing CO2 to hydrocarbons, owing to its unique electronic properties.9−11 Nevertheless, pure copper shows poor selectivity to a single hydrocarbon and inescapable hydrogen evolution activity, causing a high cost for separation and collection of the mixed product.9 To achieve high selectivity to certain desirable reduction products, the chemical state of the copper surface is engineered to tune the adsorption strength of intermediates on the catalyst. Recent studies suggest that the oxidation state of copper on the catalyst surface has a significant influence on the CRR pathway and the product composition.11−18 Compared with metallic Cu0, the oxidized
copper species (Cuδ+) exhibit higher binding strengths to Cbound intermediates, which promotes the activation of CO2 and the subsequent hydrogenation.19−21 Our previous study on Cu4.16CeOx catalysts have demonstrated that cuprous ions facilitate the yield rate of ethylene, while cupric ions are related to methane production.22 Hopefully, methane selectivity can be tuned by controlling the oxidation state of copper. However, surface Cuδ+ sites are readily reduced to Cu0
under CRR working conditions, especially at high reducing potentials, leading to the obvious drop in C1 or C2+ production.23,24 Over the past few years, several strategies have been proposed to stabilize the Cuδ+ species, including plasma treatment,25,26 element doping,21,27,28 support effect,29,30 ligand effect,31 and space limiting effect;32 nevertheless, the active Cuδ+ species are still reduced easily after the prolonged electroreduction. Therefore, it remains a challenge to stabilize Cuδ+ species on the catalyst surface under CRR conditions. Herein, we provide a new solution by engineering a Cu/ ZnOx interface to create and stabilize Cu δ+ active sites. This new interface structure delivers a high faradic efficiency of 36% and excellent stability over 12 h to produce CH4. Through

Therefore, interface engineering shows promising prospects for improving the selectivity of CRR products.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ZnOx nanoparticles were grown on a Cu foil by magnetron sputtering followed by an oxidation−reduction treatment, and the details are given in the section Experimental Details of the Supporting Information. Briefly, zinc nanoparticles were sputtered onto the clean copper foil to obtain a Cu/Zn bimetal foil, which was sequentially immersed into a hydrogen peroxide and sodium borohydride solution for an oxidation reaction. At last, the foil was electrochemically reduced under a negative potential to obtain an oxide-derived Cu/ZnOx (ODCuZn) sample. The sputtering time and current were varied to control the coverage of ZnOx on the Cu foil to optimize the CRR performance of OD-CuZn (Figures S1 and S2). We then performed detailed characterization of the morphology and structure of OD-CuZn catalysts after the CO2 electroredution test. Figure 1a shows the scanning
electron microscopy (SEM) image of the optimized ODCuZn catalyst obtained by sputtering for 100 s under a current of 30 mA. It is found that many nanoparticles are uniformly deposited on the Cu surface, with the size ranging from 30 to 100 nm. The side-view SEM image also reveals the successful deposition of hemispherical nanoparticles on the surface of the Cu foil (Figure 1b). To show the element distribution as much as possible, a line scan was performed using high-magnification SEM on the surface of OD-CuZn (Figure 1c). It can be seen that copper has a uniform distribution with high content in the
selected area, while the content of Zn increases in the area where nanoparticles exist. Thus, it can confirm that a copper surface decorated by many nanoparticles composed of Zn is constructed in the OD-CuZn catalyst. The OD-CuZn catalyst (Figure S3) and particles scraped from the Cu foil (Figure 1d) were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD) before and after the CRR test. As shown in Figure 1d, the intensity of ZnO diffraction peaks becomes weak after CO2 reduction, showing that most of the oxides are reduced to metallic zinc. Nevertheless, ZnO diffraction peaks in these Zn-based particles can still be detected at 31.7 and 56.6° (PDF #36-1451), indicating that Zn and a small amount of ZnO coexist under CRR condition; this finding is consistent with previous reports.33−35 In brief, ZnOx nanoparticles are uniformly decorated on the Cu foil in the OD-CuZn catalyst. Next, the electrocatalytic activities of OD-CuZn and control samples (a pure copper foil and an oxide-derived copper foil are named Cu and OD-Cu, respectively) were measured in a CO2-saturated KHCO3 solution. The gaseous products are monitored at applied potentials ranging from −0.7 to −1.3 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) (Figure S4). Figure 2 shows the CRR selectivity toward CH4 and C2H4 for
OD-CuZn, OD-Cu, and Cu. The OD-CuZn catalyst preferentially generates CH4 over C2H4 under the working conditions (Figure 2a). OD-CuZn achieves up to 36.1% methane faradic efficiency (FE) at −1.1 V versus RHE, almost 4-fold that of the OD-Cu, while the FE of C2H4 was significantly reduced to 16%. Furthermore, the energy efficiencies of these catalysts were examined. The OD-CuZn catalyst exhibits a maximum CH4 formation energy efficiency (EE) of 7.46%, which is 3.44 and 5.97 times higher than those of OD-Cu and Cu (Figure 2b). The enhancement in FE and EE toward methane on OD-CuZn reveals that the presence of ZnOx promotes the formation of CH4 and suppress C−C bond coupling. Additionally, the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA)-corrected LSV curves were measured to explore the intrinsic activity of the as-prepared catalysts (Figure S5). As
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c04718 Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2021, 60, 273−280
274
shown in Figure 2c, the ECSA-corrected current density of OD-CuZn is significantly larger than those of OD-Cu and the Cu foil at all potentials. In particular, OD-CuZn reaches an ECSA-corrected current density of 4.14 mA/cm2 at −1.1 V versus RHE, where the highest CH4 production selectivity is achieved. Long-term electrocatalysis was conducted to explore the stability of the OD-CuZn catalyst. Obviously, the OD-CuZn catalyst shows superior stability for CH4 and C2H4 production. The total current density for OD-CuZn is relatively stable, decaying only 7% within 12 h. In particular, the FE of CH4 on OD-CuZn remains 31−35% at −1.1 V versus RHE. However, a dramatic drop in selectivity toward CH4 and C2H4 is seen for the OD-Cu catalyst after 5 h (Figure S6). The difference in stability is partially due to the morphology evolution during the stability test. OD-CuZn can maintain its Cu/ZnOx interface structure, while the nanosheet morphology of ODCu is destroyed after the durability test (Figure S7). To magnify the effect of the interface structure on the selectivity toward CH4, we etched the OD-CuZn electrode with acid to remove ZnOx, and resultantly, the CH4 selectivity reduces dramatically to the extent of the pure Cu foil, revealing that ZnOx plays a crucial role in the high selectivity of CH4 (Figure S8). For further confirmation, a series of OD-CuZn electrodes were prepared by varying the size and number of the ZnOx nanoparticles (Figures S1 and S2). A volcano-type relationship of methane FE with the sputtering time is seen (Figure S9a). This relationship indicates that CH4 selectivity is related to the coverage of ZnOx nanoparticles on the copper surface, which reaches the optimal value at a sputtering time of 100 s. Besides, there exists a negative correlation between methane FE and the sputtering current (Figure S9b). The increasing sputtering current leads to the formation of larger ZnOx nanoparticles on the Cu foil, and thus the area of the Cu/ZnOx interface and its adjacent region would be decreased. Thus, the interface structure of Cu/ZnOx is of great importance to the performance of methane production. To explore the effect of the Cu/ZnOx interface on the CH4 production activity, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) characterization were carried out. Cu+ and Cu2+ with their characteristic satellite peaks are clearly observed for OD-CuZn and OD-Cu after CO2 reduction (Figure 3a,b). OD-CuZn has a relatively higher intensity Cu2+ peak at 934.5 eV than OD-Cu,36 and the ratio of Cu2+ to Cu+ (Cu2+/Cu+) on OD-CuZn is 1.28 according to the integration of the Cu 2p XPS peak areas, whereas the Cu2+/Cu+ ratio of OD-Cu is as low as 0.26. This difference demonstrates that OD-CuZn has more surface Cu2+ than ODCu. Additionally, in XPS O 1s spectra (Figure 3c), the O peaks at 529.9 and 530.5 eV are consistent with the binding energies of lattice oxygen in CuO and Cu2O/ZnO,
36,37 respectively, further confirming the different copper valences in OD-CuZn and OD-Cu. To investigate the relationship of selectivity with the surface Cu state, we plot the FEs of CH4 and C2H4 as a function of the content of surface Cu2+ (Figure 3d). The content of surface Cu2+ was determined by the ratio of Cu2+ to the sum of Cu0, Cu+, and Cu2+, calculated by the integral value for the XPS peak area (Table S1). After the CRR test, the surface contains 56.3% Cu2+ for OD-CuZn and 20.2% Cu2+ for OD-Cu, while no Cu2+ exits in the Cu sample. Obviously, there is a positive correlation between methane FE and the content of surface Cu2+ species. As the content of surface Cu2+ increases, the FE
of CH4 increases continuously at various potentials, while the FE of C2H4 first increases and then decreases. These results imply that cupric species favor the protonation of adsorbed CO to generate CH4 and suppress the production of C2H4. Besides, the catalysts after 10 h of the CRR test were also detected by XPS and AES, and the results indicate that cuprous and cupric ions were heavily reduced in OD-Cu, whereas preserved well in OD-CuZn (Figure S10). Therefore, it is believed that stable cupric ions in the OD-CuZn catalyst are responsible for the efficient and stable production of CH4 gas. To investigate the real chemical state of the samples during the CRR process, we have conducted in situ Raman spectra characterization for OD-CuZn and OD-Cu. In situ Raman spectroscopy measurement was performed on these samples in a CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte, while they were being subjected to a constant potential of −1.1 V. Figure 4 shows the surface chemical state of OD-CuZn and OD-Cu at the beginning of the CRR test, after 2 h of the test, and after 5 h of the test, respectively. OD-CuZn has obvious characteristic peaks of Cu2+(292 and 340 cm−1) at the beginning of the reaction, and these characteristic peaks can still be observed after 5 h of the reaction (marked in Figure 4a), indicating that cupric species were stable in OD-CuZn. On the contrary, although OD-Cu has both Cu+ and Cu2+ initially, there are hardly any characteristic peaks of copper ions after 2 h of the reaction, demonstrating that OD-Cu is easier to be reduced than ODCuZn under the CRR test environment. Thus, in situ Raman spectroscopy further proved that Cu2+ can exist stably in the OD-CuZn catalyst. Indeed, the original OD-CuZn catalyst has bulk structures of ZnOx anchored on the copper oxide foil, so they cannot be directly characterized in high-magnification microscopic characterization such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Therefore, we prepared powders of simulated catalysts (ZnOx anchored on copper oxide nanoparticles), which have similar structures to our OD-CuZn catalysts, for better
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c04718 Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2021, 60, 273−280
275
characterization of the interface structure. To investigate the Cu/ZnOx interface structure more clearly, we sputtered Zn on Cu particles and then followed the same procedure for ODCuZn to prepare a simulated catalyst. After the CRR test, the Cu/ZnOx interface in the simulated catalyst was directly observed by high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) and analyzed by energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) mapping. In Figures 5a and S11, it can be seen that ZnOx particles are anchored onto the copper surface tightly, forming a Cu/ZnOx interface. Noticeably, the O element can also be detected obviously in the area which is rich in Cu but poor in Zn (marked by the frame in Figure 5a). These observations confirm that the surface copper atoms around the Cu/ZnOx interface are slightly oxidized. Combining XPS, AES, and in situ Raman spectra results of OD-CuZn after CO2 reduction (Figures 3a,b, 4a, and S11), we
can conclude that the Cu/ZnOx interface helps preserve Cu δ+ ions (especially cupric ions), which are most likely to be the key active sites for producing CH4. Figure 5b−h shows a possible mechanism for generating CH4 at the Cu/ZnOx interface. The linear CO2 molecule is captured and activated by a cupric site, forming a bent adsorbed CO2 molecule (Figure 5b). Next, the adsorbed CO2 can initially hydrogenate to a *COOH intermediate with the aid of a H2O molecule (Figure 5c) and then dissociate to produce adsorbed *CO (Figure 5d). Further, the adsorbed *CO is directly hydrogenated at O centers to form *COH and *COH2 (Figure 5e) and then dehydrated to form a *C intermediate via the cleavage of the C−O bond (Figure 5f). Subsequently, *CH, *CH2, and *CH3 species are formed by *C by further serial hydrogenation (Figure 5g), and finally CH4 desorbs from the cupric site on the catalyst surface (Figure 5h).38
Next, we performed DFT calculations to explore the correlation between copper oxidation states and their methane selectivity. We build atomic models of (111) surfaces for Cu, Cu2O, and CuO catalysts.
39−43 On the (111) surface of CuO, there are two kinds of copper atoms that are bonded with three O (Cu3) and four O atoms (Cu4) (Figure S12a). Considering that Cu4 atoms are nearly saturated, we select the Cu3 atoms as the adsorption sites. Similarly, in Cu2O, there are also two kinds of copper atoms (Cu1 and Cu2) and we select Cu2 atoms as the adsorption sites (Figure S12b). It is popularly accepted that methane evolves from CO2 via two possible pathways, namely, via *CHO (pathway I) and *COH (pathway II).38,44−46 Commonly, the hydrated proton in the electrolyte can be captured by the O tip of the adsorbed CO radical on copper to form *COH, while adsorbed *H over the Cu surface prefers to connect with the C atom to form *CHO.47,48 Considering the (111) facet of Cu, *COH are more stable than *CHO with the involvement of the solvated protons;38,47
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c04718 Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2021, 60, 273−280
276
we thus adopted the pathway II for calculation, as reported in the previous literature.44,47 The selectivity of CO2 electroreduction depends strongly on the formation and further reduction of the *CO intermediate, so we compare the Gibbs free energies for the reduction of CO to CH4 on (111) facets of Cu, Cu2O, and CuO (Figures 6 and S13 and Table S2). For the Cu catalyst, the adsorption, hydrogenation of *CO, and the generation of *C species from adsorbed *COH are all endothermic, and the protonation of *CO is the rate-limiting step with a maximum ΔG of 1.37 eV. By contrast, the ratelimiting steps for Cu2O and CuO catalysts are both *CO adsorption, and the formation of *CO over the CuO surface with an energy barrier of +0.56 eV is much lower than that for Cu2O (+0.87 eV), demonstrating that Cu
2+ ions can bind the *CO intermediate more tightly than Cu+ ions. Therefore, these theoretical results illustrate that the generation of CH4 is more favorable on the surface with Cu2+, which are consistent with the above catalytic properties of OD-CuZn. Meanwhile, we also calculated the Gibbs free energy of
producing the C2H4 product pathway for the three samples (Cu, Cu2O, and CuO) in the CRR process. In addition to the continued protonation of *CH2 to form *CH3 and CH4, a C− C coupling reaction may occur with adjacent *CH2 to generate the C2H4 product when *CH2 is formed on the copper site. Figure 7a,c compares the changes in the Gibbs free energy for a *C2H4 species formed by a pair of *CH2 on the surfaces of Cu, Cu2O, and CuO. It can be seen that Cu has the highest
barrier (2.53 eV), while the barrier for CuO is lower (2.07 eV) and Cu2O has the lowest (1.56 eV), which is also in line with the experiment results that Cu+ is beneficial to the formation of C2H4 products. Thus, Cu
2+ can promote the formation of methane and inhibits the formation of ethylene. To further understand how the interface structure of ODCuZn stabilizes the existence of Cu2+, we performed DFT calculations to calculate the CuO and CuO−ZnO structures (Figures 8 and S14). The differential charge density diagram in Figure 8a illustrates that after the formation of the CuO−ZnO interface, electron transfer occurs around the CuO−ZnOx
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.0c04718 Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2021, 60, 273−280
277
interface, which leads to the strong interaction between CuO and ZnOx that can effectively stabilize such ZnOx−CuO interface. On the other hand, the electronic structures of Cu, Zn, and O atoms (marked in Figure S14) on the surfaces of CuO and CuO−ZnO were achieved in the density of states (DOS) plot shown in Figure 8b. It can be seen that Cu 3d, O 2p, and Zn 3d orbitals overlap strongly with the introduction of ZnOx in CuO−ZnO, so there are strong interactions between Cu, Zn, and O atoms. Such a strong interaction is able to reduce the energy of the material system and plays a role in the stability of the structure. Thus, it may be the reason why Cu2+ is more stable in the OD-CuZn interface structure. It is worth noting that oxide-derived CuZn has been reported for CO2RR with high alcohol selectivity because these catalysts, which contain appropriate metallic Zn, can provide adequate free CO to finish the insertion process between Cu− C-bound intermediates and complete the C−C coupling.34,49 In our OD-CuZn catalyst, the content of Zn is much lower (4 wt % according to SEM-EDS) and the interface structure of Cu/ZnOx can stabilize Cu
2+ for a long time to promote the protonation of *CO to form methane, so the products of CO2 reduction reaction are different.
■ CONCLUSIONS A Cu foil loaded with ZnOx nanoparticles was engineered for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to methane. The maximum faradic efficiency of methane is ∼36% at 1.1 V (vs RHE), and there is no significant decay within 12 h during the long-term durability test. At the Cu/ZnOx interface, ZnOx species induce cupric ions, which serve as highly active sites for methane formation. Meanwhile, the Cu/ZnOx interface stabilizes the cupric species during the electroreduction reaction and gives rise to long-term durability. The synthesis method of this catalyst does not require precise and harsh preparation conditions like previous traditional laboratory materials, and the process is simple and convenient with a low cost and a short production cycle. It is hoped that mass production of methane can be achieved by directly increasing the area of the catalyst foil. In addition, interface engineering, which we proposed to adjust the chemical states on the catalyst surface, can also be applied to other kinds of materials and probably arouse some inspiration for chemical engineering.
